newsitem.title: USA: Unions love America's gambling mecca.
newsitem.headline: Unions love America's gambling mecca.

text.p: Las Vegas, America's gambling mecca, is fast becoming the capital of organised labour, poised to surpass New York as the U.S. city with the most union members compared to the number of jobs available.

The city of glitz and glamour has been a focal point of this week's annual winter conference of the executive council of the AFL-CIO in Los Angeles, a success story that leaders hope will galvanise the labour movement in its recruiting efforts.

Heavy construction in Las Vegas is 100 percent unionized, as are supermarkets, while the gaming industry is about 80 percent unionized. AFL-CIO president John Sweeney said the city was about to supplant his native New York as "the heartbeat of the American labour movement."

John Wilhelm, General Secretary-Treasurer of the Hotel Employees and Restaurant Employees International Union, said at least 30 percent of the work force in Las Vegas was unionized, compared to 14.5 percent nationwide.

Wilhelm, who organised the membership drive for his union's Las Vegas local, where membership has risen from 18,000 to 45,000 in the last 10 years, told Reuters secrets to success were throwing out old union practices and ways of thinking and forming "marriages" with hotels and casinos.
"We threw out all the union bugaboos. There's no featherbedding, there are no stupid job classifications that are dysfunctional and we did away with the famous union work rules," he said.

Instead, organised labour in the gaming, hotel, heavy construction and supermarket industries "worked very hard to figure out how it is that you negotiate labour agreements that protect and enhance the standard of living of our members on the one hand, but are streamlined and flexible enough to ensure that the employers can grow and be profitable on the other hand," Wilhelm said.
Las Vegas, he added, was "an interesting laboratory for the rest of the country" because it was an entirely service-based economy, "and that of course is where the American economy is going."

He said Las Vegas proved it was possible to have a rapidly growing, highly profitable, service-based metropolitan economy which, because it was unionized, "provides a very acceptible standard of living even though the workforce has a relatively low level of formal education and technical training."

So don't be fooled by the cocktail waitress in fishnet tights. She could be a shop steward like Margaret Jane Turney, who helped organised the Santa Fe hotel and casino, which had been paying its employees $2 an hour or less.

She and her colleagues won their battle when a court ruled in December that a ballot among employees 3-1/2 years ago showing a vast majority wanted to join the hotel workers union was valid. Contract negotiations are due to begin next month.
